### Problem: Contains Duplicate III {#sec-lts-p5-b}

::: {.p-statement}

Given `nums` ($2 \le n \le 10^5$, $-10^9 \le \mathit{nums}[i] \le 10^9$) and integers $\mathit{indexDiff} \ge 1$, $\mathit{valueDiff} \ge 0$, decide whether some pair of *distinct* indices $i, j$ satisfies $|i - j| \le \mathit{indexDiff}$ **and** $|\mathit{nums}[i] - \mathit{nums}[j]| \le \mathit{valueDiff}$.

Source: [LC 220 · Contains Duplicate III](https://leetcode.com/problems/contains-duplicate-iii/){.solved difficulty="Hard"}

Example — `nums = [1,2,3,1], indexDiff = 3, valueDiff = 0`. Output `true` (pair $(0,3)$: same value, index gap $3 \le 3$).
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Brute force checks every pair inside the index window — $O(n \cdot \mathit{indexDiff})$. The linear trick comes from bucketing by *value*: make each bucket exactly $\mathit{valueDiff} + 1$ wide, so **any two numbers in one bucket are automatically within** $\mathit{valueDiff}$. Then a valid value-pair can only be a same-bucket collision or two neighbours, and keeping only the last $\mathit{indexDiff}$ elements in the buckets turns "is a value-close partner still live?" into a hash lookup — the pigeonhole of @sec-lts-a4, now indexed by value range instead of array slot.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Window scan.** For each $i$, compare against the next $\mathit{indexDiff}$ entries; return true on the first value-close pair. $O(n \cdot k)$ time, $O(1)$ space — the oracle.
2. **Value buckets.** Width $w = \mathit{valueDiff} + 1$, bucket id $b = \lfloor x / w \rfloor$ (floor division, also for negative $x$). Keep a hash map from bucket id to the value stored there, holding only the last $\mathit{indexDiff}$ elements. For each new $x$: a hit in bucket $b$ is an answer; a value in bucket $b - 1$ or $b + 1$ is an answer if it is within $\mathit{valueDiff}$. Otherwise store $x$ in bucket $b$, and once $i \ge \mathit{indexDiff}$ delete the bucket of `nums[i - indexDiff]`, which has just left the window. $O(n)$ expected time, $O(\min(n, \mathit{indexDiff}))$ space.

**Invariant.** Before element $i$ is processed, the map holds exactly the elements with indices in $[i - \mathit{indexDiff}, i - 1]$, **one per bucket**: two window elements in one bucket would differ by less than $w$, so the scan would already have stopped. Any partner within $\mathit{valueDiff}$ of $x$ lies in bucket $b - 1$, $b$ or $b + 1$, so three probes see every candidate.
:::

The buttons are in order: scan the window directly, then let value-width buckets collapse the search to a few probes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Window scan

::: {.form-next}
For every index, test the $\mathit{indexDiff}$ elements ahead of it and stop at the first pair whose values differ by at most $\mathit{valueDiff}$. $O(n \cdot k)$ time, $O(1)$ space — correct and the baseline.

**Worked example.** at $i=0$, look ahead 3: `nums[3]=1`, $|1-1| = 0 \le 0$ → `true`.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def cd220_brute(nums, indexDiff, valueDiff):
    n = len(nums)
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i + 1, min(i + indexDiff + 1, n)):
            if abs(nums[i] - nums[j]) <= valueDiff:
                return True
    return False
```

##### C++

```cpp
// compare each element with the indexDiff entries after it
bool cd220Brute(const vector<int>& nums, int indexDiff, int valueDiff) {
    int n = (int)nums.size();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n && j <= i + indexDiff; ++j)
            if (llabs((long long)nums[i] - nums[j]) <= valueDiff) return true;
    return false;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** The inner bound `min(i + indexDiff + 1, n)` enforces $|i-j| \le \mathit{indexDiff}$ by construction, so only the value test remains. `llabs((long long)...)` in C++ prevents overflow when two $\pm 10^9$ values are subtracted. Worst case $n = 10^5$ with $k$ large is $O(nk)$ — too slow, which is what the buckets fix.

#### Value buckets (linear expected)

::: {.form-next}
Bucket by $\lfloor x / (\mathit{valueDiff}+1) \rfloor$; a same-bucket hit is automatically close, a neighbour bucket needs the value check. Keep the map windowed to the last $\mathit{indexDiff}$ elements by deleting the one that falls out. $O(n)$ expected time, $O(\min(n, \mathit{indexDiff}))$ space.

**Worked example.** `nums = [1, 5, 9, 1, 5, 9, 4]`, $\mathit{indexDiff} = 2$, $\mathit{valueDiff} = 3$, so $w = 4$ and the ids are $0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 1$. Indices $0..5$ find nothing close in the window (the second `1` meets only `5` and `9`, too far in value). At index $6$, $x = 4$ has id $1$, and bucket $1$ holds the `5` from index $4$: a hit, `true`.
:::


::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-lts-220-bucket
def cd220_bucket(nums, indexDiff, valueDiff):
    w = valueDiff + 1
    seen = {}                                   # bucket id -> the one live value in it
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        b = x // w                              # floor division, also for negatives
        if b in seen:
            return True
        if b - 1 in seen and x - seen[b - 1] <= valueDiff:
            return True
        if b + 1 in seen and seen[b + 1] - x <= valueDiff:
            return True
        seen[b] = x
        if i >= indexDiff:
            del seen[nums[i - indexDiff] // w]  # that element leaves the window
    return False

for _ in range(1500):
    nums = [random.randint(-12, 12) for _ in range(random.randint(2, 18))]
    k = random.randint(1, len(nums))
    t = random.randint(0, 6)
    assert cd220_bucket(nums, k, t) == cd220_brute(nums, k, t)
assert cd220_bucket([1, 2, 3, 1], 3, 0) is True
assert cd220_bucket([1, 5, 9, 1, 5, 9], 2, 3) is False
assert cd220_bucket([1, 0, 1, 1], 1, 2) is True
assert cd220_bucket([1, 5, 9, 1, 5, 9, 4], 2, 3) is True    # the board sample
assert cd220_bucket([-1, 1], 1, 1) is False             # floor ids keep -1 and 1 apart
print("cd220_bucket OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
// bucket by valueDiff+1, probe same and neighbour buckets, window by index
bool cd220Bucket(const vector<int>& nums, int indexDiff, int valueDiff) {
    long long w = (long long)valueDiff + 1;
    auto id = [&](long long x) { return x >= 0 ? x / w : (x + 1) / w - 1; };   // floor division
    unordered_map<long long, long long> seen;   // bucket id -> the one live value in it
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)nums.size(); ++i) {
        long long x = nums[i], b = id(x);
        if (seen.count(b)) return true;
        auto l = seen.find(b - 1);
        if (l != seen.end() && x - l->second <= valueDiff) return true;
        auto r = seen.find(b + 1);
        if (r != seen.end() && r->second - x <= valueDiff) return true;
        seen[b] = x;
        if (i >= indexDiff) seen.erase(id(nums[i - indexDiff]));
    }
    return false;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** Width $w = \mathit{valueDiff}+1$ is the whole trick: two values in the same bucket differ by less than $w$, so a same-bucket hit needs no value check, while a neighbour bucket *can* straddle the boundary and gets the explicit test. Because a bucket never holds two live values, the map stores the value itself, and the window is kept by deleting exactly one bucket per step: the bucket of the element that just aged out. (Scanning the whole map for stale entries instead would cost $O(\mathit{indexDiff})$ per step and lose the linear bound.) The ids must come from **floor** division: C++ `/` truncates toward zero, which would put $-1$ and $1$ into the same bucket $0$ even with $w = 2$ and break the one-per-bucket invariant, so the C++ computes the floor by hand; the assert on `[-1, 1]` (answer `false`) pins that case. Both versions keep values in 64-bit integers so $10^9 - (-10^9)$ cannot overflow.

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Window scan** is $O(n \cdot \mathit{indexDiff})$ time, $O(1)$ space. **Value buckets** is $O(n)$ expected time (three hash probes, one insert and one delete per element), $O(\min(n, \mathit{indexDiff}))$ space. A sliding ordered set (`std::set` with `lower_bound`) gives $O(n\log k)$ in the worst case, with no hashing involved.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- $\mathit{valueDiff} = 0$ forces an exact value match; a bucket holds only identical values, so same-bucket is sufficient.
- Very large $\mathit{valueDiff}$ makes $w$ large and buckets sparse — the map stays tiny and the neighbour check does the real work.
- Negative values: the bucket id must be a true floor, $\lfloor x / w \rfloor$; truncating division merges the buckets on both sides of zero.
:::

::: {.practice}
- [LC 219 · Contains Duplicate II](https://leetcode.com/problems/contains-duplicate-ii/){difficulty="Easy"} — the special case `valueDiff = 0`: one bucket per value, a window of the last $k$ indices.
- [LC 2817 · Minimum Absolute Difference Between Elements With Constraint](https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-absolute-difference-between-elements-with-constraint/){difficulty="Medium"} — index gap at least $x$ instead of at most $k$; buckets no longer suffice, an ordered set does.
:::
